231.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital. … The capital is human life, the gain is heaven; through the loss of that capital man must be born as a denizen of hell or a brute animal.”
231.explanation: Mahāvīra's parable of the three merchants treats human life as capital: virtue earns a profit, mere decency only preserves the capital, and sin loses it.
231.tie_back: Valluvar says giving and a praiseworthy life are the only real profit a person can earn from living. The Jain parable likewise treats a human life as an investment whose only true gain is a good life's reward, not wealth.
231.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
231._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; both texts share the 'only true profit of life' framing, but the Jain gain is a heavenly rebirth through virtue, not renown or giving specifically.

232.quote_or_event: “In the sky sounded drums, intoxicating by their echoes, like bards proclaiming Śreyāṃsa’s happiness.” … The kings, townsmen, and the other people … said to Śreyāṃsa: “O Prince, you are fortunate, a crest-jewel of men, since you persuaded the Master to accept even a little cane-juice.”
232.explanation: When Prince Śreyāṃsa offered sugar-cane juice to break the first Tīrthaṅkara Ṛṣabha's year-long fast, gods and men together celebrated the giver. Jain tradition holds that the duty of giving on earth began with this act.
232.tie_back: Valluvar says all the praise that speakers utter comes to rest on those who give; in this Jain story, the praise of gods, kings and townspeople likewise gathers on the giver Śreyāṃsa.
232.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), ch. III, part 7 'The fast-breaking of Ṛṣabha' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
232._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (ellipses mark omissions). A strong narrative parallel, though the praise centres on a gift to a Jina rather than to ordinary suppliants.

233.quote_or_event: “Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
233.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī reminds King Iṣukāra that at death every possession is left behind, and only dharma goes with a person.
233.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing in this world lasts except matchless renown. The Jain text also picks out one thing that survives impermanence, but that thing is dharma, not fame.
233.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
233._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the shared structure (only one thing endures) is close, but Jain renunciant ethics does not value worldly renown, so the enduring thing is different.

234.quote_or_event: “…because he stands fast in midst of dangers and fears, patiently bears hardships and calamities, adheres to the chosen rules of penance, is wise, indifferent to pleasure and pain, rich in control, and gifted with fortitude, the name Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra has been given him by the gods.”
234.explanation: The Kalpa Sūtra says the gods themselves gave Vardhamāna the name 'Mahāvīra' because of his human virtues. In Jain cosmology the gods honour and serve the Tīrthaṅkaras, and liberation can only be reached from a human birth.
234.tie_back: Valluvar imagines the celestial world honouring a renowned human above its own sages. Jain tradition holds something similar, with gods naming, praising and serving a human Jina whose achievement exceeds their own.
234.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §108 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
234._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com (opening ellipsis marks an omitted clause). The gods-honour-a-human idea is a genuine Jain parallel, but the honour goes to ascetic virtue, not to earthly renown.

235.quote_or_event: “These two ways of life ending with death have been declared: death with one's will, and death against one's will. Death against one's will is that of ignorant men, and it happens (to the same individual) many times. Death with one's will is that of wise men, and at best it happens but once.”
235.explanation: Mahāvīra's lecture on death contrasts the fool's repeated, unwilling deaths with the wise person's single, willing death, which can bring the cycle of rebirth to an end.
235.tie_back: Valluvar says a loss that is really gain, and a death that is really living on, are within reach only of the wise. The Jain text likewise reserves a death that is a victory rather than a loss for the wise alone.
235.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.2–3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
235._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com. Both texts make a good death the achievement of the wise only, but the Jain fruit is liberation or a higher birth, not survival in renown.

236.quote_or_event: “Death devours your days, using the sun from which they originate as the measure by which he metes them. Practise therefore virtue and be compassionate, for such as do not act thus, though they are born, must be esteemed as unborn.”
236.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār says that those who live without virtue and compassion may as well never have been born.
236.tie_back: Valluvar says that if one is born, one should be born with the qualities that bring renown, and that otherwise it is better not to be born. The Nālaṭiyār passes the same verdict, that a birth without virtue counts as no birth.
236.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 7 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
236._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this Tamil Jain text closely matches the 'better unborn' logic, but names virtue and compassion rather than renown as what gives a birth value.

237.quote_or_event: “By repenting of one's sins to oneself the soul obtains repentance, and becoming indifferent by repentance he prepares for himself an (ascending) scale of virtues, by which he destroys the Karman resulting from delusion.”
237.explanation: In Jain practice, self-reproach for one's own faults (nindā) and confessing them before a teacher (garhā) are regular disciplines that purify the soul.
237.tie_back: Valluvar tells those who lack renown to grieve over themselves instead of resenting their critics; Jainism likewise makes blaming oneself, not others, a path to moral growth.
237.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.6 (cf. 29.7) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
237._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com. Inward self-reproach fits the kural's turn from blaming others to blaming oneself, though the Jain context is repentance for sin, not failure to win renown.

238.quote_or_event: “Neither his kinsmen, nor his friends, nor his sons, nor his relations will share his suffering, he alone has to bear it; for the Karman follows the doer.”
238.explanation: The monk Citra tells King Brahmadatta that at death nothing goes with a person except the karma they have earned.
238.tie_back: Valluvar calls renown the proper legacy (eccam) that a life leaves behind. The Jain answer is that what remains of a life is the karma it carries forward, not a name left among others.
238.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.23 (cf. 13.24) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
238._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com. Both texts ask what remains of a life, but the Jain answer (karma, which the doer carries on) is different from social renown left behind; this is a next-best match.

239.quote_or_event: “From the moment that this our boy has been begotten, our silver increased, our gold increased, &c. … Now our wishes have been fulfilled, therefore shall the name of our boy be Vardhamâna.”
239.explanation: Mahāvīra's parents named him Vardhamāna, 'the Increaser', because their household prospered from the moment he was conceived.
239.tie_back: Valluvar says the land that carries a renownless person sees its harvest fail. The Kalpa Sūtra tells the reverse story, in which a virtuous soul's presence makes the family's wealth and grain increase.
239.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §§106–107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
239._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com (the '&c.' is Jacobi's). This is an inverse, narrative parallel only; Jain karma theory does not hold that a bad person's presence blights the land.

240.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.” “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse with much profit to him who acts up to the Law.”
240.explanation: The young sons of the priest Bhṛgu tell their father that every passing day is lost for good, and that its worth depends on whether it was lived righteously.
240.tie_back: Valluvar separates those who truly live from those who merely stay alive. The Jain verses draw the same line, saying that only days lived by the Law bear fruit.
240.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
240._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi notes the original says 'nights'). The two texts share the contrast between real and wasted living, but the measure is dharma, not freedom from blame and possession of renown.
